notes.meaning: Moses is told to speak to the entire congregation of Israel, not just the priests. God commands all His people to be holy—set apart from evil and devoted to Him—because the Lord their God is holy. His own perfect goodness is the standard and pattern for how His people must live.

Children are told to respect and obey their mother and father, and all Israelites must keep the Sabbath, God's weekly day of rest. Mothers are named first here because small children spend so much time with them and might easily take them for granted. Honoring parents and keeping God's sacred day form the foundation of a faithful home and society.

The Lord commands His people never to turn to idols or cast statues of false gods. The Hebrew word used for idols literally means "nothings," showing that images made by human hands have no life or power. Leaving the living God to worship useless figures is foolish and disloyal.

A peace offering was a voluntary sacrifice brought to celebrate fellowship and give thanks to God. The person bringing it had to offer it willingly and follow God's rules so it would be accepted. The meat could be eaten on the day of the sacrifice or on the next day, but anything left by the third day had to be burned up.

Eating any of the peace offering on the third day made the sacrifice spoiled and unacceptable to God. Because the meat had been set apart for the Lord, treating it like common, rotting leftovers dishonored what was holy. Anyone who ate it carried their own guilt and was cut off from the covenant community.

During harvest time, landowners were forbidden from reaping all the way to the edges of their grain fields. In the vineyards, farmers could not pick every last grape or gather the fruit that dropped to the ground. These leftovers were reserved for the poor and for foreigners so they would not go hungry.

God commands His people not to steal, cheat, or lie to one another. Taking what belongs to someone else destroys trust, and lying often follows stealing to cover up the wrongdoing. Honest words and fair dealing keep a community peaceful and safe.

No one was allowed to swear an oath using God's name to support a lie. Calling on God to back up dishonesty drags His holy name into disgrace. Honoring the Lord means speaking the truth in every promise and statement.

Defrauding or robbing a neighbor by force or trickery is strictly forbidden. Employers were not allowed to hold back the daily pay of a hired worker until the next morning. Day laborers owned no land and relied on each day's pay to feed their families that evening.

The law forbids cursing someone who is deaf or placing an obstacle in front of someone who is blind. A deaf person cannot hear an insult to answer it, and a blind person cannot see a trap to avoid falling. God demands deep reverence toward Himself because He sees how people treat the defenseless and will defend them.

Judges were commanded never to twist justice in a legal dispute. They could not rule unfairly out of soft pity for a poor person, nor could they favor a wealthy person out of fear or greed. Every case had to be decided strictly on truth and fairness.

Spreading rumors and talking behind people's backs was entirely prohibited. The word used for a slanderer pictures a peddler carrying gossip from house to house. God also forbade doing anything that put a neighbor's life in danger, such as giving false testimony in a court trial.

God commands His people not to nurse secret hatred in their hearts against a fellow countryman. Instead of staying silent in bitterness, a person was to talk directly and kindly to the neighbor about their wrong. Speaking up gives the wrongdoer a chance to repent and prevents the silent person from sharing in the blame.

Taking revenge or holding on to a grudge against a countryman is forbidden. Instead, the Lord calls His people to love their neighbors as they love themselves, sincerely wanting what is good for them. This command is the foundation of biblical love and treatment of other people.

Israelites were commanded to respect the boundaries God set in the created world. They could not crossbreed different kinds of farm animals, sow two different seeds in the same plot, or wear clothing made by weaving wool and linen together. These everyday rules served as constant reminders that God's people were set apart and must not blend true worship with pagan practices.

This rule addresses a man who sleeps with an enslaved woman who is promised in marriage to another man but has not yet been bought out or freed. In normal adultery involving a free woman, the penalty was death, but here death was not required because the woman was an enslaved person without full control of her situation. Instead, an investigation and physical punishment took place so the wrong was not left unaddressed.

Even though the man was spared the death penalty, he was still guilty of sin before God. He was required to bring a ram to the entrance of the tabernacle as a guilt offering. The priest offered the ram to make atonement—meaning to provide cleansing and make peace with God—and the man was forgiven.

When Israel entered Canaan and planted fruit trees, they were not allowed to eat the fruit for the first three years, treating it as unharvested and set aside. In the fourth year, the whole crop was dedicated to the Lord as an offering of praise. By the fifth year, the owner could eat the fruit freely, trusting God's blessing to make the orchard produce even more in the future.

Eating meat with the blood still left in it was strictly forbidden. God also outlawed fortune-telling, witchcraft, and watching for signs to predict good or bad luck. Seeking secret guidance through occult arts showed a lack of trust in God's care and providence.

The people were forbidden from shaving the sides of their hair, shaping their beards into heathen patterns, cutting their skin, or putting tattoo markings on their bodies for the dead. Neighboring nations performed these acts during funerals and pagan ceremonies to appease false gods. God's people were to honor the bodies He made and mourn with hope rather than copy pagan rites.

Parents were commanded never to push their daughters into prostitution, a shameful practice commonly used in pagan idol worship. Forcing young women into such wickedness would cause depravity to spread across the whole land. God demanded that families remain pure and guard the dignity of their children.

The Lord repeats the command to keep His Sabbath rest and show deep respect for His sanctuary. Gathering for worship on God's holy day protected the people from drifting into the corrupt practices of surrounding nations. It kept their hearts centered on the holy God who lived in their midst.

Israel was warned never to consult mediums or spiritists who claimed to talk with the dead for hidden guidance. Turning to occult practitioners made a person spiritually unclean and showed disloyalty to the Lord. God's people were to look only to Him and His revealed word for truth.

Younger people were commanded to stand up in respect before the elderly and honor those with grey hair. In the ancient world, old age was valued for wisdom and seen as a special blessing from God. Treating older people with honor is directly tied to fearing and respecting God Himself.

Israelites were forbidden from mistreating or taking advantage of foreigners living among them. They were told to treat the foreigner just like a native-born Israelite and love him as themselves. God reminded them of their own past as helpless strangers in Egypt, calling them to show the mercy they once needed.

Cheating in trade by using false measurements for length, weight, or volume was strictly outlawed. Sellers had to use honest scales, accurate stone weights, and true containers like the dry ephah and liquid hin. The Lord who rescued them from slavery required complete fairness and honesty in daily business.

The Lord closes these laws by calling Israel to obey all His decrees and commands faithfully. God's great goodness in saving His people gave them a loving duty to follow His rules. Walking in obedience was the true and fitting way to honor the God who redeemed them.
